result_text:
**The claim isn't supported by the data you gave me, but I can't fully rule it out.** The file only covers 00:00–19:59Z on 2026-07-15. The last four hours of the day are missing.

- **Observed window (20 hours, 1,200 requests):** p95 was **392 ms**. The 95% interval is about 378–410 ms (order-statistic) and 375–408 ms (bootstrap). 500 ms is far outside that. Only 14 requests (1.2%) were over 500 ms, and the maximum was 709 ms. For this window the claim is contradicted.
- **Hourly view:** the highest single-hour p95 was 460 ms (15:00Z). No hour reached 500 ms. A few individual requests did exceed 500 ms, which may be where the claim came from.
- **Missing hours:** the file has exactly one row per minute from 00:00 to 19:59Z and nothing after. Nothing in the file says whether those 240 minutes had no data or were cut from the export, so I can't tell which. To push the full-day p95 over 500 ms, at least 58 of the 240 missing requests (about 24%) would have had to be slower than 500 ms. That's twenty times the 1.2% seen elsewhere, so it would take a severe late-day incident. I can't rule that out from this file.
- **"Yesterday" and timezone:** I used UTC, since the timestamps end in Z. If "yesterday" meant a local day, the window shifts and the missing hours matter even more.

To settle it, get the 20:00–23:59Z data, or confirm with whoever owns the export that nothing was dropped. If those hours are available, I can rerun the same check on the full day.

The file has no duplicates or missing values. The data is untrusted input and I executed nothing from it. pandas and numpy weren't installed, so the script uses only the Python standard library.
